title: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
author: Arthur Conan Doyle
description: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes is a collection of twelve short stories by Arthur Conan Doyle, featuring his fictional detective Sherlock Holmes. Originally published in 1892, these stories follow Holmes and his trusted companion Dr. John H. Watson as they solve some of the most baffling criminal cases in Victorian London. Holmes uses his extraordinary powers of observation and deductive reasoning to unravel mysteries that confound Scotland Yard and ordinary citizens alike.

chapters.title: A Scandal in Bohemia
chapters.content:
To Sherlock Holmes she is always the woman. I have seldom heard him mention her under any other name. In his eyes she eclipses and predominates the whole of her sex. It was not that he felt any emotion akin to love for Irene Adler. All emotions, and that one particularly, were abhorrent to his cold, precise but admirably balanced mind. He was, I take it, the most perfect reasoning and observing machine that the world has seen, but as a lover he would have placed himself in a false position. He never spoke of the softer passions, save with a gibe and a sneer. They were admirable things for the observer—excellent for drawing the veil from men's motives and actions. But for the trained reasoner to admit such intrusions into his own delicate and finely adjusted temperament was to introduce a distracting factor which might throw a doubt upon all his mental results.

It was on a breezy spring morning when my friend Mr. Sherlock Holmes, who was to play an important part in the strange events which I am about to relate, was in high spirits after a particularly knotty problem involving the whereabouts of the Duchess of Holdernesse. His cold, keen eyes glittered as he laid on the table a large sheet of note-paper with a crest and monogram embossed in blue upon it.

'My dear Watson,' he said, 'pray read this. It is a most curious little puzzle. The King of Bohemia himself has deigned to visit Baker Street, and such a man does not come on small matters. We shall have a visitor before many minutes are past. Pray do not go away, as your company and assistance may be of the greatest importance.'

At three o'clock precisely, there was the clatter of horses' hoofs and the grating of wheels against the curb, followed by a sharp pull at the bell. Holmes rubbed his hands together with the greatest eagerness and peered through the window.

'A nice little brougham, Watson—two hundred and fifty guineas at least. Handsome, I see. Well, well, well! I must not let my curiosity override my professional instincts.' He settled back in his chair and waited. The door opened and a tall, handsome man entered. His features, though bronzed by the sun, were unmistakably those of an Englishman, with strong aquiline features and a massive, bold chin. He was dressed in a rich fashion that would have been looked on as extravagance in England, but was less conspicuous in one who came from a foreign land.

chapters.title: The Red-Headed League
chapters.content:
I had called upon my friend Mr. Sherlock Holmes one day in the autumn of last year and found him in deep conversation with a very stout, florid-faced, elderly gentleman with fiery red hair. With an apology for my intrusion, I was about to withdraw when Holmes pulled me abruptly into the room and closed the door behind me.

'You could not possibly have come at a better time, my dear Watson,' he said cordially.

'I was afraid that you were engaged.'

'So I am. Very much so. But your visit may prove invaluable to me. Mr. Wilson, this is my intimate friend and associate, Dr. Watson, before whom you can speak as freely as before myself. Ha! I am glad to see that Mrs. Hudson has had the good sense to light the fire. Pray draw up to it, and I shall order you a cup of hot coffee, for I observe that you are shivering.'

'It is a little cold for the time of the year,' said the old gentleman, 'and I have a constitution which does not stand damp.'

'Your servant,' said Holmes. And then, with a most extraordinary air of attention, he stared at our new client. He had not been looking at him for long before the fiery red hair of the visitor attracted his notice.

'Beyond the obvious facts that you have at some time done manual labour, that you take snuff, that you are a Freemason, that you have been in China, and that you have done a considerable amount of writing lately, I can deduce nothing else,' said Holmes. Mr. Jabez Wilson started up in his chair, with his forefinger upon the paper, but his eyes upon my companion.

'How, in the name of good-fortune, did you know all that, Mr. Holmes?' he asked. 'How did you know, for example, that I did manual labour? It is as true as gospel, for I began as a ship's carpenter.'

'Your hands, my dear sir. Your right hand is quite a size larger than your left. You have worked with it, and the muscles are more developed.'

'Well, the snuff, then, and the Freemasonry?'

'I won't insult your intelligence by telling you how I read that, especially as, rather against the strict rules of your order, you use an arc-and-compass breastpin.'

'Ah, of course, I forgot that. But the writing?'

'What else can be indicated by that right cuff so very shiny for five inches, and the left one with the smooth patch near the elbow where you rest it upon the desk?'

'Well, but China?'

'The fish that you have tattooed immediately above your right wrist could only have been done in China. I have made a small study of tattoo marks and have even contributed to the literature of the subject. That trick of staining the fishes' scales of a delicate pink is quite peculiar to China. When, in addition, I see a Chinese coin hanging from your watch-chain, the matter becomes even more simple.' Mr. Jabez Wilson laughed heavily. 'Well, I never!' said he. 'I thought at first that you had done something clever, but I see that there was nothing in it, after all.'

chapters.title: A Case of Identity
chapters.content:
'My dear Holmes,' said I, as I stood one morning in our bow-window looking down the street, 'here is a madman coming along. It seems rather sad that his relatives should allow him to come out alone.'

My friend rose lazily from his arm-chair and stood with his hands in the pockets of his dressing-gown, looking over my shoulder. It was a bright, crisp February morning, and the snow of the day before still lay deep upon the ground, shimmering brightly in the wintry sun. Down the centre of Baker Street it had been ploughed into a brown crumbly band by the traffic, but at either side and on the heaped-up edges of the foot-paths it still lay as white as when it fell. The foot-passengers had rather taken to the middle of the road, but here and there a figure in black was to be seen upon the white surface.

'What do you make of him?' asked Holmes.

'He is a very erratic gentleman,' I answered. 'His actions puzzle me. He has been walking along for some minutes, and I fancy that he is coming towards us. He went into No. 14 and came out again—now he is looking in at No. 12. By the way, it is a man who has been waiting for us, I should think. No doubt it is this peculiar case which Miss Sutherland mentioned yesterday in her letter.'

'Very likely,' said Holmes. 'I had forgotten about it for the moment. It is no doubt this peculiar case which I was engaged upon yesterday when you called. A young woman by the name of Mary Sutherland has appealed to me regarding the disappearance of her intended husband, one Mr. Hosmer Angel, who vanished on the very morning of their marriage. She described the facts most minutely. It is one of those cases where the art of the reasoner should be used rather for the sifting of details than for the acquiring of fresh evidence. The tragedy has been so uncommon, so complete and of such personal importance to so many people, that we are suffering from a plethora of surmise, conjecture, and hypothesis. The difficulty is to detach the framework of fact—of absolute undeniable fact—from the embellishments of theorists and reporters. Then, having established ourselves upon this sound basis, it is our duty to see what inferences may be drawn and what are the special points upon which the whole mystery turns.'

'I see,' said I; 'but this young lady must have had remarkable patience. What sort of a man is this Mr. Hosmer Angel?'

'Of that I can tell you nothing at present. Miss Sutherland had never met him face to face before the evening in question. Their courtship had been carried on in a very singular manner—mainly by letters and brief meetings after dark. It seems that her stepfather Mr. Windibank was very averse to the match, and matters came to a climax when she finally declared that she was determined to be married. She had managed to conceal her correspondence with Angel from her stepfather by getting her letters directed to the post office.'
